title: Biological pigment
wiki_lead:
A biological pigment, also known simply as a pigment or biochrome, is a substance produced by living organisms that have a color resulting from selective color absorption. Biological pigments include plant pigments and flower pigments. Many biological structures, such as skin, eyes, feathers, fur and hair contain pigments such as melanin in specialized cells called chromatophores. In some species, pigments accrue over very long periods during an individual's lifespan.
Pigment color differs from structural color in that it is the same for all viewing angles, whereas structural color is the result of selective reflection or iridescence, usually because of multilayer structures. For example, butterfly wings typically contain structural color, although many butterflies have cells that contain pigment as well.

Biological pigments
See conjugated systems for electron bond chemistry that causes these molecules to have pigment.

Heme/porphyrin-based: chlorophyll, bilirubin, hemocyanin, hemoglobin, myoglobin
Light-emitting: luciferin
Carotenoids:
Hematochromes (algal pigments, mixes of carotenoids and their derivates)
Carotenes: alpha and beta carotene, lycopene, rhodopsin
Xanthophylls: canthaxanthin, zeaxanthin, lutein
Proteinaceous: phytochrome, phycobiliproteins
Psittacofulvins: a class of red and yellow pigments unique to parrots
Turacin and Turacoverdin: red and green pigments found in turacos and related species
Anthoxanthins: white color of some plants
Other: melanin, urochrome, flavonoids


Pigments in plants

The primary function of pigments in plants is photosynthesis, which uses the green pigment chlorophyll and several colorful pigments that absorb as much light energy as possible. Pigments are also known to play a role in pollination where pigment accumulation or loss can lead to floral color change, signaling to pollinators which flowers are rewarding and contain more pollen and nectar.
Plant pigments include many molecules, such as porphyrins, carotenoids, anthocyanins and betalains. All biological pigments selectively absorb certain wavelengths of light while reflecting others.
The principal pigments responsible are:

Chlorophyll is the primary pigment in plants; it is a chlorin that absorbs blue and red wavelengths of light while reflecting a majority of green. It is the presence and relative abundance of chlorophyll that gives plants their green color. All land plants and green algae possess two forms of this pigment: chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b. Kelps, diatoms, and other photosynthetic heterokonts contain chlorophyll c instead of b, while red algae possess only chlorophyll a. All chlorophylls serve as the primary means plants use to intercept light in order to fuel photosynthesis.
Carotenoids are red, orange, or yellow tetraterpenoids. During the process of photosynthesis, they have functions in light-harvesting (as accessory pigments), in photoprotection (energy dissipation via non-photochemical quenching as well as singlet oxygen scavenging for prevention of photooxidative damage), and also serve as protein structural elements. In higher plants, they also serve as precursors to the plant hormone abscisic acid.
Betalains are red or yellow pigments. Like anthocyanins they are water-soluble, but unlike anthocyanins they are synthesized from tyrosine. This class of pigments is found only in the Caryophyllales (including cactus and amaranth), and never co-occur in plants with anthocyanins. Betalains are responsible for the deep red color of beets.
Anthocyanins (literally "flower blue") are water-soluble flavonoid pigments that appear red to blue, according to pH. They occur in all tissues of higher plants, providing color in leaves, plant stem, roots, flowers, and fruits, though not always in sufficient quantities to be noticeable. Anthocyanins are most visible in the petals of flowers of many species.

grok_lead: Biological pigments are naturally occurring chemical compounds produced by living organisms that selectively absorb certain wavelengths of visible light while reflecting or transmitting others, thereby imparting distinctive colors to tissues, organs, and structures. These pigments are synthesized across a wide range of taxa, including plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms, and play essential roles in processes such as photosynthesis, protection from environmental stressors, and interorganismal communication. In plants, prominent examples include chlorophylls, which enable light absorption for energy conversion; carotenoids, such as Î²-carotene and lutein, which serve as accessory pigments in photosynthesis and antioxidants; anthocyanins, responsible for red, purple, and blue hues in flowers and fruits; and betalains, nitrogen-containing pigments unique to certain families like the Caryophyllales that provide yellow to red-violet coloration. Carotenoids are synthesized via the 2-C-methyl-D-erythritol 4-phosphate (MEP) pathway in plastids, forming eight isoprenoid units, while anthocyanins belong to the flavonoid class with a C6-C3-C6 structure, and betalains derive from betalamic acid as immonium derivatives. In animals, biological pigments often reside within specialized cells called chromatophores and include melanins, which produce black or brown shades for UV protection and camouflage; carotenoids acquired through diet, such as astaxanthin in fish for vibrant reds and antioxidant effects; and pterins or purines like guanine in iridophores for iridescent or metallic appearances. For instance, in ornamental fish, melanophores contain melanin for dark pigmentation, erythrophores hold reddish carotenoids, xanthophores display yellow hues from xanthophylls, and leucophores reflect white light using crystalline structures. Animals typically cannot synthesize carotenoids de novo, relying instead on dietary sources like algae or plankton, with supplementation enhancing coloration intensity. Microbial pigments, such as prodigiosins in bacteria like Serratia, violacein in Chromobacterium, and phycobiliproteins in cyanobacteria, exhibit similar light-absorbing properties and contribute to biodiversity in coloration. The functions of biological pigments extend beyond aesthetics, encompassing critical survival mechanisms. In photosynthetic organisms, chlorophylls and carotenoids facilitate light harvesting and energy transfer in photosystems, while also dissipating excess energy to prevent oxidative damage through cycles like the xanthophyll cycle. Anthocyanins and betalains act as antioxidants, provide UV screening, and signal to pollinators or seed dispersers by attracting animals with vivid colors, thereby aiding reproduction and ecological interactions. In animals, pigments enable camouflage against predators, sexual signaling for mate attraction, and physiological protection, such as melanin shielding against solar radiation or carotenoids supporting immune responses. Bacterial pigments often confer advantages in extreme environments, including antimicrobial activity, viral resistance, and adaptation to oxidative stress, highlighting their evolutionary significance across kingdoms. Overall, these compounds not only define the visual diversity of life but also underpin vital biochemical pathways, with ongoing research exploring their applications in nutrition, medicine, and biotechnology.
